questions.question: Which of the following is the action of the muscle inserted to the area marked below?
questions.explanation: The marked insertion is on the mandible for the lateral pterygoid muscle. The action of this muscle is depression, protrusion and side-to-side movement of the jaw. Lateral pterygoid originates from the infratemporal surface and infratemporal crest of the greater wing of sphenoid and from the lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate. It inserts into the pterygoid fovea, capsule of the temporomandibular joint and articular disc.

questions.chapter: Muscles, Neurovascular Anatomy of Head & Neck
questions.question: A 26-year-old man presented with the inability to close his mouth after yawning. On evaluation, there is an anterior dislocation of the temporomandibular joint. This condition is caused by the excessive contraction of which of the following muscles?
questions.explanation: Anterior temporomandibular-joint dislocation occurs due to excessive contraction of the lateral pterygoid, classically with extreme mouth opening such as yawning, laughing, vomiting or dental treatment. Some fibers of the upper head of the lateral pterygoid insert into the capsule of the TMJ and the anterior/medial borders of the articular disc. Contraction can pull the disc forward; excessive opening can cause anterior displacement of the joint. Superior and posterior dislocations are rare and associated with high-energy trauma.

questions.question: An elderly woman presents to you with the following findings. She gives a history of chickenpox in her childhood. Which of the following is false about the cranial nerve involved in this case?

options.text: Motor innervation is exclusively carried by maxillary division
Its cornea is primarily innervated by ophthalmic division
It provides motor supply to medial pterygoid

questions.correctAnswerText: Motor innervation is exclusively carried by maxillary division
questions.explanation: The findings are suggestive of herpes zoster involving the trigeminal nerve. The false statement is that motor innervation is exclusively carried by the maxillary division. Motor fibers are carried by the mandibular division. The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is the largest cranial nerve and has ophthalmic (V1), maxillary (V2) and mandibular (V3) divisions. V1 supplies sensation to the scalp, cornea, conjunctiva, iris, upper eyelid, lacrimal gland, forehead and mucous membranes of the nose. V2 supplies lower eyelid, cheeks, maxillary sinus, nasal cavity, lateral nose, upper lip, palate, teeth and gingiva. V3 supplies sensation to the chin/lower lip, temporal membrane, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric and mandibular teeth, and provides motor supply to the muscles of mastication, tensor veli palatini and tensor tympani.

questions.question: A dentist provides local anesthesia by injecting lidocaine at the site marked X to block a division of the trigeminal nerve. Which of the following muscles is not supplied by the trunk of this nerve?
questions.explanation: The site marked X is the mandibular foramen containing the inferior alveolar nerve, a branch of the mandibular nerve. The muscles medial pterygoid, tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini are supplied by the nerve to medial pterygoid, which arises from the trunk of the mandibular nerve. Lateral pterygoid is supplied by a branch from the anterior division of the mandibular nerve.

questions.question: A patient with past history of parotidectomy now presents with sweating and flushing of skin over the cheek during mastication. Which of the following nerves is involved in this case?
questions.explanation: The presentation is Frey's syndrome, involving the auriculotemporal nerve, marked 2. The other numbered structures are maxillary nerve, posterior auricular nerve and inferior alveolar nerve. The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the posterior division of mandibular nerve and provides cutaneous sensation to the tragus and adjoining external acoustic meatus and to the auricle/scalp. It carries postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid. After parotid surgery, aberrant regeneration of these fibers to sweat glands and skin vessels causes gustatory sweating, warmth and redness during salivation.

questions.question: In which of the following compartments of temporomandibular joint do the rotatory movements of the jaw take place?

options.text: Joint space above the articular disc
Joint space below the articular disc
Joint space medial to the articular disc

questions.correctAnswerText: Joint space below the articular disc
questions.explanation: Rotatory movements of the jaw take place in the joint space below the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint. The temporomandibular joint is adapted to both gliding and rotary movement. The capsular ligament around the upper compartment is relatively loose and allows gliding/translation, while the lower compartment is tighter and allows rotational movement.

questions.question: A patient with diplopia was found to have paralysis of the muscle marked below. What is its nerve supply?
questions.explanation: The marked muscle is the superior oblique muscle. It is supplied by the trochlear nerve (CN IV). Superior oblique helps in looking downward and inward. There are seven extraocular muscles: levator palpebrae superioris, four recti, and two obliques. Lateral rectus is supplied by abducens (VI), superior oblique by trochlear (IV), and the remaining extraocular muscles by oculomotor (III).

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman comes to the Ophthalmology OPD with complaints of a right-sided squint. On asking her to look straight, you observe the following. What is the nerve supply of the muscle paralyzed in this case?
questions.explanation: The medial rectus is paralyzed on the right side, leading to unopposed action of the lateral rectus and a divergent/lateral squint. Medial rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique are supplied by the inferior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III). Oculomotor nerve has superior and inferior divisions in the orbit; superior division supplies superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris, while inferior division supplies inferior rectus, medial rectus and inferior oblique.

questions.question: A 43-year-old woman presented with hyperacusis. She recently underwent reconstructive surgery for fracture of mandible at the TMJ. Investigations revealed paralysis of the stapedius muscle. A branch of which of the following nerves is likely to cause the given condition?
questions.explanation: Stapedius is supplied by the nerve to stapedius, a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII). Injury causes stapedius paralysis and hyperacusis because stapedius and tensor tympani normally contract in response to loud noises to dampen vibration of the tympanic membrane and reduce oscillation of the ossicles. Paralysis increases sensitivity to sounds.

questions.question: Identify the thickened nerve marked in the arrow in the image shown below:
questions.explanation: The thickened nerve marked by the arrow is the great auricular nerve. The other visible nerve is the transverse cervical nerve. The great auricular nerve is the largest ascending branch of the cervical plexus and arises from the second and third cervical spinal nerves. It winds around the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid and ascends, dividing near the parotid into anterior and posterior branches. It supplies skin over the mastoid region, posteroinferior auricle, parotid region and angle of mandible. Clinical points include sensory loss after injury, Frey's syndrome relationship, and use in nerve grafting.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a hybrid muscle?
questions.explanation: The sternohyoid muscle marked as 3 is not a hybrid muscle. It is innervated only by the anterior rami of spinal nerves C1-C3 via ansa cervicalis. Examples of hybrid muscles in the figure include trapezius and sternocleidomastoid, which receive motor supply from the spinal accessory nerve with proprioceptive fibers from cervical spinal nerves, and digastric, whose anterior and posterior bellies have different nerve supplies.

questions.question: The carotid angiography of a 30-year-old with a carotid body tumor shows splaying at the bifurcation of the carotids as seen in the image below. At what level do you expect to find this?
questions.explanation: The carotid bifurcation is at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, approximately C3-C4. The right common carotid arises from the brachiocephalic trunk and the left directly from the arch of aorta. In the neck, each is enclosed in the carotid sheath with the internal jugular vein and vagus nerve and divides into internal and external carotid arteries. Clinical points include carotid bifurcation stenosis/atherosclerosis, carotid sinus hypersensitivity and endarterectomy.

questions.question: The only branch of the external carotid artery which is given from its medial side is:
questions.explanation: The only branch of the external carotid artery given from its medial side is the ascending pharyngeal artery. The external carotid begins at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage around C4 and gives superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital and posterior auricular arteries before terminating as maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.

questions.question: A patient with a history of cavernous sinus thrombosis died of an arterial ischemic stroke. An autopsy revealed carotid artery narrowing. Which of the following branches of the internal carotid artery will not be involved in this case?
questions.explanation: Cavernous sinus thrombosis may narrow the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery. Branches arising from the cavernous part include meningeal artery, inferior hypophyseal arteries and branches to the trigeminal ganglion. The ophthalmic artery is not a cavernous-part branch and therefore is not involved in the described lesion.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man presented to the ER with a history of a head injury following an RTA. CT head revealed a displaced fracture of the floor of the middle cranial fossa, involving the pterygoid canal. Which of the following nerves are susceptible to injury?

options.text: Lesser petrosal nerve and greater petrosal nerve
Greater petrosal nerve and deep petrosal nerve
Greater petrosal nerve and chorda tympani
Lesser petrosal nerve and deep petrosal nerve

questions.correctAnswerText: Greater petrosal nerve and deep petrosal nerve
questions.explanation: The pterygoid canal is formed by fusion of postganglionic sympathetic fibers of the deep petrosal nerve and preganglionic parasympathetic fibers of the greater petrosal nerve. The nerve of the pterygoid canal (Vidian nerve) traverses this canal from the middle cranial fossa to the pterygopalatine fossa. It carries autonomic fibers ultimately distributed to lacrimal and nasal mucous glands; hence a fracture involving the canal can injure the greater and deep petrosal components.

questions.question: The artery passing through the structure marked A is a branch of ______ part of the maxillary artery.
questions.explanation: The marked structure is the pterygoid canal. The artery of the pterygoid canal is a branch of the pterygopalatine (third) part of the maxillary artery. Branches of the pterygopalatine part include posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital, greater palatine, pharyngeal, artery of pterygoid canal and sphenopalatine arteries.

questions.question: A patient with tricuspid regurgitation has an engorged neck vein as shown in the given image. What are its formative tributaries?

options.text: Posterior auricular vein and retromandibular vein
Superficial temporal vein and maxillary vein
Retromandibular vein and deep facial vein

questions.correctAnswerText: Posterior auricular vein and retromandibular vein
questions.explanation: The image shows distension of the external jugular vein. Its formative tributaries are the posterior auricular vein and the posterior division of the retromandibular vein. Facial/scalp venous drainage: superficial temporal and maxillary veins join to form retromandibular vein; its anterior division joins facial vein to form common facial vein draining into internal jugular; its posterior division joins posterior auricular vein to form external jugular vein, which drains into the subclavian vein.

questions.question: Which of the following is a part of the dangerous area of the face?

options.text: Middle third of the upper lip
Middle third of the lower lip
Lateral third of the lower lip

questions.correctAnswerText: Middle third of the upper lip
questions.explanation: The dangerous area of the face is the triangular area extending from the corners of the mouth to the bridge of the nose, including the nose and maxilla. Therefore the middle third of the upper lip is included. Facial vein communicates with cavernous sinus through superior ophthalmic vein and pterygoid venous plexus; facial infection can spread intracranially and cause cavernous sinus thrombosis.

questions.question: The correct pair of lymph node level in the neck and anatomical boundaries amongst the following are:

options.text: Level 5 - Base of skull to cricoid

questions.explanation: The correct pair is level 6 - hyoid to clavicle. The source groups cervical lymph nodes by level: level 1 submental/submandibular; level 2 upper jugular; level 3 middle jugular; level 4 lower jugular; level 5 posterior triangle; level 6 anterior group; level 7 mediastinal. The accompanying diagram shows lateral-view neck node levels.
